N the middle of December last year, 
tae Shanghai Municipal Council and 
the French Municipal Council issued a 
jot proclamation in which they 
threatened to expel from the areas 
within their jurisdiction people who 
manipulate the prices of rice. «This 
measure was taken on ‘the ground that 
profiteering in rice, the staple food of 
the Chinese populace, menaces the pub- 
lie safety and welfare of Shanghai. 


At the time that the proclamation 
was made public, this newspaper stated 
that the step was a laudable official 
gesture, but its ultimate usefulness 
would depend upon the rigid enforce- 
ment of the order promulgated by the 
Concession and the Settlement govern- 
ing body. The fact that the price of 
rice hus registered another sharp in- 
crease and that it is slated for a fur- 
ther rise would indicate that there is a 
need on the part of the two Councils 
to take further substantial measures to 
put teeth into their December pro- 
+ elamation. 
: " * s . 


"JHE increase in the price of rice is 
not the only disturbing factor in 

- the local commodity situation. The 
price of soft coal, according to a report 
appearing in this newspaper, is likely 
lo reach $3850 a ton. At the same time, 
other daily necessities such as vege- 
‘ables, meat, oil, and clothing ‘have all 
vhown a tendency of further increases. 


Evidently the price situation today, 
heck: 


cannot be ¢ by piecemeal adjust- 
ment. If any result is to be achieved 
at all, it can be achieved only by giving 
consideration to the question of com- 


veetables and other daily necessities 


Furthermore, in dealing with the! 
question of commodity prices, the two, 
Councils must also abandon — their 
former view that the problem 
essentially of an emergency and tem-| 
eorary nature, and that consequently the | 
remedial measures devised need only be! 
of a stop-gap variety. The situation 
today shows that the question of high 
living costs and high commodity prices 
has come for an extended stay’ in 
Shanghai, and to solve the problem th¢« 
two Councils must take a INERT range | 
view of the issue. 


is

@ 
a this connection, it may also b 

necessary for the two Councils to 
devise proper ways to overcome the 
handicap of their limited legal autho- 
rity. If the power which the Shanghai 
Municipal Council possesses by virtue 
of the Land Regulations is not sufficient 
to cope with the present crisis, then 
vroper steps must be taken until this 
legal obstruction is refoved. The 
commodity price question affects the} 
welfare of so many millions of people 
and it is of so serious a nature that 
‘egal pbstruction must not be allowed 
to remain as an excuse or reason for 
official inaction. 


This newspaper is reasonably op‘ 
vnistic that if a required amount of er 
thusiasm and determination exists 
among the officials of the local yovern- 
ing organization, something can he 
done to check. at least partially, the 
rise in commodity prices. There are a 
aumber of possible channels which ca 
he explored in this search for a wa‘ 
to remedy the present situation. A 
xnecial committee, with substantial a) 
‘hority and civic support, may be 
ganized to investigate the commodity 
vrice question in detail. If as a re- 
cvlt of this investigation, it is shown 
that a serious shortage exists «in rice, 
coal and other soods, some ways can 
he devised for the Councils to import 
the needed commodities in order to 
relieve the, shortage. These and other 
measures may come under the genera’ 
heading of “welfare enterprises.” 


On the other hand, and coming 
under the general heading of “law en- 
forcement,” the Councils may take ad- | 
ditional steps to check profiteering. The 
proclamation which was made with re- 
eard to rice profiteering should be ex 
tended to-ineclude profiteering in other. 
essential goods and services. . 


The suggestion, we have made may 
indeed sound ambitious and. .difficult.' 
But the: prese&t situation is growing: sc 
serious that :morally and legally, the 
Councils cannot dismiss the whole thing 
with the blanket phrase, “it cannot be 
done.” It is up to the two Council 
to try, and try until they succeed.’ _
